meta.title: Embedding Pipelines at Scale
meta.thesis: Embedding Pipelines at Scale is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A docs platform embeds thousands of changed pages nightly without serving stale search results. By the end, they should be able to build or review scaled embedding pipeline with queue, dedupe, and freshness checks, measure fresh searchable chunks after docs updates, and catch the failure where partial failures leave old and new embeddings mixed together.

mentalMap.title: Embedding Pipelines at Scale: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Move from source changes to versioned vectors, filtered retrieval, backfills, and migration checks.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: An embedding pipeline is a data product: every vector must be reproducible, query-compatible, filterable, monitored, and replaceable during model migrations.

blocks.title: The vector is not the source of truth

spans.text: Problem anchor: Agentic Learning Studio adds 8,000 KB chunks, updates 400 of them, and deletes 50 outdated notes. Search quality drops because old and new embeddings mix in the same collection, some deleted chunks still retrieve, and no one can tell which embedding model produced a result.

The pipeline contract fixes that. Each vector row needs a stable chunk ID, source URL, tenant or category, content hash, embedding model ID, vector dimension, distance metric, chunker version, created time, and active/deleted status. The source document remains authoritative; vectors are derived artifacts that can be rebuilt.

items.text: Product framing: freshness means learners retrieve current approved notes, not stale drafts.
Engineering framing: idempotent upserts, tombstones, and versioned collections make retries safe.
Evaluation framing: a model migration is allowed only after recall tests compare old and new indexes on the same queries.

spans.text: That row gives every downstream system something to check. The worker can skip unchanged content hashes. The vector store can reject wrong dimensions. The retriever can filter to approved sources. The migration job can create `kb_bge_v2` without corrupting active retrieval.

blocks.title: Spot the missing contract field
blocks.prompt: Which field most directly prevents mixing embeddings from two model families?

options.text: The document title alone.
The embedding model version and vector dimension.
The worker host name.

blocks.explanation: Titles help humans, but compatibility is determined by model, dimension, normalization, and distance metric.

blocks.title: Queues scale only when retries are safe

spans.text: Embedding work fails in ordinary ways: rate limits, GPU memory pressure, malformed documents, vector-store timeouts, and schema mismatches. If a retry creates a second ID or activates a partial collection, search quality becomes a data consistency problem.

Treat ingestion as a state machine. Source changed, chunked, embedded, upserted, verified, activated, and tombstoned are separate states with owners. A failed worker should resume from the last durable state, not guess which chunks it already wrote.

chunker version, content hash, source offset

options.name: Embed

cells.text: Batch chunks through one encoder contract
model ID, dimension, normalization, worker version

options.whenToUse: When content hash is new or model version changes.

options.name: Activate

cells.text: Move verified collection or rows into retrieval
recall test report and rollback collection
half the corpus uses the new model and half the old one

options.whenToUse: After backfill and retrieval checks pass.

spans.text: A team swaps from a 384-dimensional model to a 768-dimensional model. New chunks go into a new collection, but query-time code still embeds with the old model for one endpoint. The system passes insert tests and fails user search in subtle ways: similar-looking chunks rank oddly, filters still work, and only evaluation catches recall loss.

The fix is procedural: activate model, query encoder, collection, distance metric, and eval report as one versioned bundle. Do not let document updates silently choose the new model before the query path does.

modules.title: Choose storage around filters and migrations
modules.sub: Pick vector storage by operational boundary, metadata filters, recall tests, and rebuild cost.
modules.summary: The vector store is part of the pipeline contract; it decides how filtering, snapshots, and re-embedding will be operated.
objectives: Compare pgvector, Qdrant, managed stores, and distributed stores by job.
Explain why metadata filters are not optional in RAG.
Plan a recall test against exact or trusted retrieval.

spans.text: A small Postgres-native corpus can start in pgvector because SQL filters, backups, and app data live together. A dedicated retrieval service such as Qdrant makes sense when filtered vector search is its own scaling boundary. Managed services reduce operations but still require IDs, metadata, snapshots, and migration plans.

Two framings keep the choice honest. The product framing asks whether retrieval can respect tenant, freshness, and approved-source filters. The platform framing asks who owns snapshots, index build time, payload schema, recall testing, and rollback when a model changes.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Choose the simplest store that can enforce filters and survive re-embedding.
blocks.useWhen: Use a dedicated vector service when retrieval volume, metadata filters, snapshots, or independent scaling are first-order needs.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid changing stores to fix weak chunk IDs, missing metadata, or absent evaluation; those problems travel with the data.

blocks.title: Check dimensions and stable upserts

spans.text: The check is intentionally small: it proves that dimension, model identity, payload, and stable IDs are present before the vector-store client writes anything. Production code would add batch retry, tombstone handling, and recall evaluation.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What happens if a 768-dimensional vector reaches a collection declared for 384 dimensions?
predictThenReveal.answer: A correct store or guard rejects the insert. If the check is missing, the failure may show up later as broken retrieval, failed upserts, or mixed collections during migration.

spans.text: AI-generated ingestion code often looks plausible while omitting lifecycle details. Review for stable IDs, content hashes, model and chunker versions, vector dimensions, delete handling, backpressure, retry idempotence, payload filters, and activation gates.

items.text: Can the code re-run the same document without duplicating vectors?
Does it keep deleted or unapproved sources out of active retrieval?
Does query-time encoding use the same compatible contract as document-time encoding?
Is there a recall test comparing old and new collections before cutover?

blocks.title: Migration gate
blocks.prompt: What is the safest way to migrate to a new embedding model?

options.text: Insert new vectors into the old collection whenever a document changes.
Build a new versioned collection, test recall and filters, then switch the query path and collection together.
Change only the query encoder and leave stored vectors untouched.

blocks.explanation: Embedding model changes are corpus migrations. The document path and query path must move as a tested bundle.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "How do I run embeddings as a reliable data pipeline instead of a one-off script?" Include stable chunk IDs, metadata payloads, content hashes, model dimensions, idempotent queue states, vector-store filters, recall tests, and collection rollback.
Spaced recall: the first module said the vector is a derived artifact. That idea should reappear in every operational decision: rebuildability beats clever one-time indexing.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Do not activate vectors until freshness, filters, and recall are proven.
blocks.useWhen: Use a collection when it has a manifest, complete backfill, tombstone handling, filter tests, recall report, and rollback target.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid treating a green upsert job as proof of search quality; inserts can succeed while retrieval gets worse.

spans.text: Choose one category such as RAG tooling. Produce a migration manifest, sample 25 queries, build a new collection, compare top-8 recall against the current collection, verify tenant/status filters, and write the activation and rollback commands. The deliverable is a release note, not just code.
Next rung: connect this to monitoring model drift and quality, where embeddings become one signal among live traffic, labels, and user outcomes.

gpu.label: GPU
gpu.laymanDefinition: A parallel device that can accelerate large embedding batches.
gpu.technicalNote: GPU use matters for offline backfills and high-volume embedding jobs, but the pipeline still needs idempotent queues and version tracking when work runs on CPU.

serving.label: Serving
serving.laymanDefinition: Making embeddings available to retrieval and refresh jobs.
serving.technicalNote: Here serving includes the query-time encoder path plus vector-store reads, not only the batch job that created the document vectors.

gateway.label: Gateway
gateway.laymanDefinition: The boundary between source systems, embedding workers, and vector storage.
gateway.technicalNote: A pipeline gateway validates tenant, source status, model version, and schema before allowing records into the active retrieval collection.

latency.label: Latency
latency.laymanDefinition: The delay between a source update and a retrievable fresh vector.
latency.technicalNote: At scale, latency includes queue age, chunking time, model batching, vector upsert time, index refresh, and query-time filter cost.

throughput.label: Throughput
throughput.laymanDefinition: How many chunks the pipeline can embed and index per hour.
throughput.technicalNote: Throughput is useful only when duplicate suppression, failure retries, and metadata filters keep the corpus correct.

versioning.label: Versioning
versioning.laymanDefinition: Recording the embedding model, dimension, chunker, normalization, and collection used by each vector.
versioning.technicalNote: Embedding versioning is mandatory because model swaps often require new collections or full re-embedding, not a tiny client change.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: You are designing a new embedding pipeline. Before you write a single line of ingestion code, which of the following must be locked into the vector contract?

options.text: The embedding model name, vector dimensions, and distance metric
The chunking strategy, queue depth, and retry backoff policy
The target vector store vendor and its hardware tier
The recall threshold and latency SLA for retrieval

questions.explanation: Dimensions and distance metric are structural — a mismatch between contract and store causes silent corruption or query failures, so they must be fixed before any data flows.

questions.prompt: An ingestion worker receives a document chunk it has already embedded last week. The content has not changed. What is the correct behavior in an idempotent state machine pipeline?

options.text: Re-embed the chunk anyway to keep timestamps current
Skip embedding and upsert — the existing vector is valid because the content hash matches
Delete the old vector and re-embed to avoid stale metadata
Route the chunk to the backfill collection for deferred processing

questions.explanation: A matching content hash proves the chunk's semantics are unchanged, so re-embedding wastes compute and quota — the idempotent contract says 'same hash → same vector, skip.'

questions.prompt: Your RAG system retrieves support tickets, but results keep including tickets from deprecated product lines that users never ask about. Which architectural decision most directly fixes this?

options.text: Switch from cosine similarity to dot-product distance
Increase the chunk size to dilute irrelevant content
Add metadata filters on product line to every retrieval query
Move from pgvector to a distributed store like Weaviate

questions.explanation: Metadata filters are not optional in RAG — without them, ANN search has no way to scope results to the relevant subset, so deprecated content pollutes every retrieval.

questions.prompt: You run a migration smoke test and discover that the new collection was built with 1536-dimensional vectors but your query encoder outputs 768-dimensional vectors. Describe what breaks and at what stage.
questions.acceptableAnswer: The query vector and stored vectors have incompatible shapes, so the vector store will reject the query outright (a dimension-mismatch error) or — in stores that don't validate — return meaningless similarity scores. No valid nearest-neighbor results can be returned. The break surfaces at query time, not at ingestion time, which is why a smoke test that issues a real query against the new collection must be part of every migration checklist.
questions.explanation: Dimension mismatches are silent at write time in some stores but always fatal at query time — the smoke test exists precisely to catch this before the collection goes live.

questions.prompt: After a bad model upgrade, recall drops 30% in production. Your rollback plan requires switching retrieval back to the previous collection. Which pipeline practice makes this rollback safe and fast?

options.text: Keeping the backfill collection in a separate namespace until recall is verified, then doing a hard cutover with an alias swap
Re-ingesting all documents into the old collection from the source queue
Reverting the embedding model weights in place and re-querying the same collection
Lowering the similarity threshold temporarily to recover more results

questions.explanation: Separating the backfill collection from the active retrieval path and using an alias (or pointer) swap means rollback is a single atomic redirect — no re-ingestion, no downtime.
